
=================================================================
#52 Jahee  (644)
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: danghang · tone: harbour romance (K-drama)
Logline: The quay doesn’t care that he’s a prince. She has already decided his arithmetic is sloppy.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Ten years earlier, at Silla’s only western harbour, the prince is eighteen and losing an argument with a tide book.
[1] ¶ Yushin sent him here for the season, to work under Kim Seonpum, who runs the quay. No yard. No horses. Grain ships, tide marks, and sums that will not close.
[2] [PLACE danghang: Silla’s only door to the western sea. Everyone knows which door.]
[3] [MAP 644: ]
[4] ¶ Seonpum has a daughter who keeps his inkstones. Her name is Jahee. She has watched the prince for three days, and she has already decided his arithmetic is sloppy.
[5] [CARD Jahee: A harbour girl who counts faster than the customs men.]
[6] Jahee: Your sums are wrong. / The tide does not care that you are a prince. / Count again. / While I am watching.
[7] King Munmu: …Where. / No — / Please show me.
[8] ¶ She corrects the sum with her father’s good brush. She is not supposed to touch it. She took it off his desk an hour ago, because it is the only one that writes small enough. He watches her mouth instead of the numbers, and she lets him, once.
[9] ¶ Then a rider comes down the coast road with a letter from Yushin. The army is marching west, against seven Baekje forts. The grain sails on the morning tide. Bupmin is to sail with it.
[10] King Munmu: The morning tide. / …Then the book has to close tonight.
[11] Jahee: It won’t. You’re forty sacks short, somewhere between the third ship and the fifth. / Forty sacks is a company that doesn’t eat for a week.
[12] King Munmu: Then show me where.
[13] ¶ They count until the lamp needs oil, and then by the light from the warehouse door. Somewhere around the fourth ship she stops correcting him, because he has stopped making mistakes. Neither of them knows what to do with their hands.
[14] ¶ Rain finds the eave. They stand inside a hard rain-curtain with a wet ledger between them, and almost do the stupid thing, and do not — until there is a stolen brush between their mouths, and then they do.
[15] Jahee: …That’s my father coughing. / He only coughs like that when he’s pretending not to be there. / …Which is why it has to be now. / Before the tide comes in.
[16] King Munmu: Do not close the book. / If you close it I… / will not know where to go.
[17] ¶ Seonpum coughs once from the dark and pretends he did not see a prince learning the harbour by kissing the girl who can count.
[18] ¶ They find it at the fifth ship, an hour before dawn. Forty sacks written down by somebody who never loaded them. The grain can sail on time and short, or a day late and whole.
[19] King Munmu: Load them. All forty. / I’ll take the next tide.
[20] Jahee: Yushin said the morning tide.
[21] King Munmu: Then he can hit me for it. / At least the company that eats will be his.
[22] Jahee: …And you’ll come back and fix your sums?
[23] King Munmu: Only if you’re watching.
[24] ¶ Years later the court will call her Jayi. The quay already had the true name.
[25] ── SCENE: The Western Forts ──
[26] ¶ He reaches the army a day late, with forty sacks of rice nobody else knew were missing. Yushin is waiting at the edge of the camp.
[27] Kim Yushin: You missed the tide.
[28] King Munmu: Yes, Marshal. The fifth ship was forty sacks short. I stayed and loaded them.
[29] ¶ Yushin hits him once, open-handed, because the order was the morning tide. Then he sends the forty sacks to the company that was going to go without.
[30] King Munmu: Marshal. / When I said king for all — did I mean every kingdom, or every person who bleeds for one?
[31] Kim Yushin: Ask the yard again tomorrow. / If the answer is only a speech, you are still six. / If it costs you a bruise — you are becoming Hwarang.
[32] ── SCENE: The Coronation Year ──
[33] ¶ Ten years later the bruise is long gone. The girl from the quay is the crown prince’s wife. The whole court stands in the palace yard in Tang silk to watch his father crowned.
[34] ¶ This king has a Secretariat, an emperor for a friend, and an army that answers to one brush. He means to make three kingdoms one. Everybody in the yard can feel a new age starting.
[35] ¶ Along the back row stand the oldest houses in Surabol, the six families who were here before there was a king. They wear the new robes because the Secretariat says so. They wear them like borrowed skin.
[36] The old houses: In my grandfather’s day a king wore what his grandfather wore. / In the first king’s day he came out of an egg. / Now he comes out of a Secretariat.
[37] King Munmu: Uncle. Why do they mind so much? / It’s only a robe.
[38] Alchun: Nothing in this country is only a robe, lad. / Their grandfathers chose the first king. So did mine. / Ask how the first one got here. Then you’ll know what they’re muttering about.
[39] ¶ **Silla’s newest king wears Tang silk. To see why the old houses mind, go back to a white horse kneeling in the grass…!**
